articles.headline: Missouri tightened the rules. The wait still leaves microbusiness owners vulnerable
articles.summary: Missouri's May 2026 microbusiness rules are aimed at the right problem and stop just short of solving it. They spell out what it means to majority-own and operate a license, let regulators review ownership arrangements before a license issues, require a compliance course before applying and again after the award, and make eligible owners the primary point of contact with regulators. All of that reaches the contract. None of it reaches the wait between a winning draw and an open door, which is when somebody offers to carry the license for you.
keyFacts: Missouri drew its final round of marijuana microbusiness applicants on September 9, 2026. The state received 888 applications and expects to issue approximately 77 licenses beginning in December.
Forty-six licenses from the first two rounds are active but not yet approved to operate. As of August 18, 2026, only 21 microbusinesses were operating.
Jimi Poe, a first-round winner and the first to open a microbusiness dispensary, told the division's podcast it took him two years rather than the six months he expected.

Terms to watch for: equity that vests on signature rather than delivery, a management agreement wearing a consulting label, fees calculated on gross rather than net, and standard operating procedures that do not describe your building.
Lesley Turek, the division's chief equity officer, has advised licensees to run proposed agreements past the division so regulators can flag compliance problems. It costs nothing.
The most important protection for Missouri's newest cannabis entrepreneurs may not be another rule. It may be knowing when not to sign.
articles.pullQuote: All of that reaches the contract. None of it reaches the wait.
articles.authorBioAsPublished: Adrian A. Holguin, J.D., M.B.A., is founder and president of CannaShark Consulting, a national consulting firm based in California that handles licensing, compliance and operations for cannabis operators.
articles.verifiedAgainst: Editor's final edited draft (Sept 22, 2026), approved by the author for publication without changes.

articles.headline: California Marijuana Businesses Should Act Now To Comply With New Packaging Rules That Don't Take Effect Until 2028
articles.summary: AB 2249 draws a clearer line around what California cannabis packaging, labels and ads may look like, with the new definition taking effect January 1, 2028. Because artwork is locked with the printer months before a run and boxes then sit in a warehouse, the real decision point for operators lands in the next two quarters, not in 2028.
keyFacts: Governor Gavin Newsom signed AB 2249 on August 31, 2026.
The new packaging definition takes effect on January 1, 2028.

Prohibited: cartoon characters such as dragons, unicorns or wizards; anyone who looks under 21; imagery of candy, cereal or desserts marketed to children; bubble or balloon lettering; packaging that mimics a non-cannabis product aimed at kids.
Realistic depictions of fruit that reflect an actual ingredient or growing region remain allowed.
Packaging artwork is typically locked weeks or months before a print run, so the compliance deadline arrives well before the legal one.
